article_content: BAMAKO, Mali — Mali’s military has seized control of the northern town of Kidal, marking the first time government forces have occupied the Tuareg rebel stronghold in almost a decade, according to state broadcaster ORTM on Tuesday. Mohamed Maouloud Ramadan, a spokesperson for the rebels based in neighboring Mauritania, confirmed the Malian military’s presence in Kidal. "This is a message from the transitional president to the people of Mali," said journalist Ibrahim Traore during ORTM’s news bulletin. "Today, our armed and security forces have taken control of Kidal. Our mission is not finished." Mali’s army, alongside mercenaries from the Russian military contractor Wagner, has been fighting Tuareg forces for several days to capture the town, following the withdrawal of United Nations peacekeepers two weeks ago. Separatist Tuareg rebels in the north have long sought to establish an independent state called Azawad. In 2012, the Tuareg rebels drove government forces from Kidal, triggering a series of events that led to nationwide instability. Dissatisfied soldiers later overthrew Mali’s elected president due to the handling of the Tuareg rebellion. During the resulting chaos, Islamic extremists took control of key northern towns, including Kidal, and imposed strict Sharia law. In 2013, France, Mali’s former colonial ruler, led a military intervention to remove extremist groups from power. However, these groups regrouped and launched attacks on the Malian army and UN peacekeepers over the following decade. A further military coup in 2020, led by Col. Assimi Goita, led to strained relations between Mali and its international partners. Mali’s foreign minister requested the departure of the UN peacekeeping mission, known as MINUSMA, and forces withdrew from Kidal in early November. — Associated Press writer Krista Larson in Dakar, Senegal, contributed.

Mohamed Maouloud Ramadan, opyta Mauritania-pe, ohechakuaáma oĩha ejército Mali pe Kidal-pe. "Ko’ãva transición rehegua mburuvicha remandu’a Malí retãygua-pe," he’i periodista Ibrahim Traoré ORTM maranduha rehe. "Ko árape, ñande ejército ha seguridad rehegua atyguasu oipykúi Kidal rehe. Ñande rembiapo ndopái gueteri." Mali ejército, oñondive Wagner rehegua Rusia rehegua mercenario-kuéra ndive, oñorairõ Tuareg-kuéra ndive heta ára, oñeha’ãgui ojapo Kidal rehe ogueraha rire pe ONU rembiapo’opa mokõi semana ohasa. Upe guive, ejército rehegua mburuvicha’ỹgua oipe’a presidente ojapóva Tuareg rebelión rehe mba’asy. Oiko mbeguekatúpe, extremista islámico-kuéra oipyhy umi tavaguasu yvate, Kidal reheve, omoĩ jey hese kuéra ley Sharia pokatu. Ary 2013-pe, Francia, Malí retã ypykue, omyakã peteĩ intervención militar oipe’a hag̃ua extremista-kuérape, ha upéi grupo-kuéra oñemomba’e jey ojapo ataque ejército Malí ha ONU rehegua ára ha ára. Peteĩ golpe de estado pyahu ary 2020-pe, omotenondéva coronel Assimi Goita, omoheko vai umi relación Mali ha ambue tetã rehe. Malí canciller ojerure ONU MINUSMA osẽ hag̃ua, ha umi fuerza osẽ Kidal-gui jasypateĩ ñepyrũme. — Associated Press Krista Larson, Dakar, Senegal-gui osẽkuri.

Meta has confirmed that it will launch an ad-free subscription plan for Facebook and Instagram users in Europe starting in November. According to a company blog post, users in the European Union, European Economic Area, and Switzerland can opt for the ad-free experience at €9.99 per month on the web or €12.99 per month if subscribing via iOS or Android devices. The higher price for mobile subscriptions reflects the fees charged by the Apple App Store and Google Play Store.

Users may continue to use Facebook and Instagram for free with ads. Meta emphasized its belief in an ad-supported internet, which provides people access to personalized services regardless of financial means.

Initially, the subscription will apply to all linked Facebook and Instagram accounts. However, from March 1, 2024, an additional fee of €6 per month on the web and €8 per month on iOS or Android will be charged for each extra account.

Meta stated that this step is intended to comply with evolving European regulations, including the stricter requirements of the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the Digital Markets Act. The ad-free subscription responds to recent regulatory scrutiny, such as penalties Meta faced in the EU, including criticism over Instagram’s handling of minors’ data.

Meta also clarified that while users are subscribed, their information will not be used for advertisements. This aligns with Meta’s move toward consent-based data use for advertising, as required by GDPR. The new subscription option is the first ad-free tier Meta has introduced for its social platforms, following similar moves from competitors like X (formerly Twitter).

article_content: Five years ago, the Venezuelan government embarked on a mission to resolve a historical mystery, with the assistance of a Florida man who held a crucial piece of evidence. President Hugo Chavez questioned the widely accepted belief that South American hero Simon Bolivar died of tuberculosis, and wondered if he might have been poisoned instead. Although subsequent scientific tests were inconclusive, another uncertainty lingered: the fate of a valuable collection of artifacts loaned to the government by Ricardo DeVengoechea. DeVengoechea, a photographer from Orlando, is now suing Venezuela in U.S. federal court to recover his treasured items. When Venezuela decided to investigate Bolivar’s death, verifying the identity of his exhumed remains became a key step. DeVengoechea’s family, one of Colombia’s founding lineages with close ties to Bolivar, had preserved a collection worthy of a museum—most notably, a unique medal from Peru, several signed letters, and a lock of Bolivar’s hair. Of particular interest was the hair, which could provide the necessary DNA to confirm Bolivar’s remains. In 2007, the Venezuelan government treated DeVengoechea as an esteemed guest, flying him and his artifacts to the country aboard a private jet. There, officials welcomed him warmly, and he collaborated with researchers for a month as his artifacts were examined. When he remembered additional artifacts at his home, Venezuela arranged commercial airfare for him to retrieve them. But as time passed, DeVengoechea’s communications with Venezuelan officials dwindled, according to his lawsuit filed in Miami. He only learned the outcome of the tests when they were reported in the media in July 2011. Although Venezuela had agreed to return his collection, by late 2011 his calls and letters to the Venezuelan Embassy went unanswered. In his legal filing, DeVengoechea accuses Venezuela of unlawfully retaining his property, stating, 'Venezuela's refusal to return the DeVengoechea Collection is a clear act of expropriation of DeVengoechea's personal property in violation of international law.' The Venezuelan Embassy in Washington declined to comment on the suit. According to the lawsuit, Bolivar personally gave the items to DeVengoechea’s great-great-grandfather, Joaquin de Mier. The collection also includes epaulets from the uniform of Napoleon Bonaparte, whom Bolivar reportedly met in France. Most historians agree that Bolivar died in 1830 at age 47 from tuberculosis. In 1819, he founded Gran Colombia, uniting present-day Venezuela, Colombia, Panama, and Ecuador, and is credited with promoting democracy in Latin America. Bolivar’s exhumation was televised, and President Chavez reportedly wept as the remains were uncovered. 'Bolivar is alive. Let us not see him as a dead man or as a skeleton. He is like lightning, like a sacred fire,' Chavez said, as the national anthem played and scientists revealed a skeleton on the table.

Presidente Hugo Chavez ohechaga’u umi ohechakuaáva Simon Bolívar omano hague tuberculosis-gui ha oñeinvestiga ikatúpa oñemoñuhã hague. Test científico rehegua ndojuhúi mba’eve, ha avei noñemohendái mba’éichapa Ricardo DeVengoechea ome’ẽ hague colección importante gobierno-pe. DeVengoechea, fotógrafo Orlando gua, oguereko ko’ágã peteî demanda Venezuela rehe Estados Unidos-pe oikapagui i mba’e. Hembiapo família, peteĩ kuarahy'yha Colombia gua, oguereko colección museo rehegua — peteĩ medalla Perú gua, kuatiañe’ẽ oguerahaukáva, ha peteĩ ape Bolivar rehegua. Imba’eite ha’e pe ape, oipytyvõva DNA rupi ohechauka Bolívar añeteguapehague. 2007-pe, gobierno Venezuela omotenonde chupe peteî invitado especial ramo, ogueru chupe ha i mba’ekuéra avión privado-pe. Oikove peteĩ mes investigación rehe omba’apo artefacto rehegua ndive. Iporãvéva, ohechakuaa oguerekoha ambue mba’e, Venezuela ome’ẽ chupe avión comercial ojerure rehe. Colección rehegua avei oĩ epaulet Napoleón Bonaparte rehegua, Bolivar ojuhuhague Francia-pe. Historiador mayoria he’i Bolívar omano hague 1830-pe, 47 ary rehe, tuberculosis-gui. 1819-pe, omoñepyrũ Gran Colombia (ko’ágã Venezuela, Colombia, Panamá, Ecuador), ha ojehecharamóva democracia rehe América Latina-pe. Bolívar exhumación ohechauka kuri TV-pe, presidente Chavez oñeñandu ha osapukái, 'Bolívar oikove. Ani pehecha upe omanóva, ni esqueletoramo. Oĩcha ha’e ilumina, peteĩ tata marangatu,' he’i Chávez, himno nacional ojehendu jave ha científico ohechauka hague peteî kangue mesa ári.

article_content: A Connecticut woman was arrested after allegedly leaving a six-year-old child alone in a car that reached an estimated 140 degrees while she got her nails done. Rasheena Francis, 28, is accused of leaving the child in East Hartford for up to two hours. A passerby saw the boy in the car around 1:30 p.m. and alerted police, according to NBC Connecticut. When authorities arrived, the car was off and the windows were rolled up. Police say Francis left the boy while she received a manicure at Lena's Nails on Burnside Avenue in East Hartford. The child was taken to Connecticut Children's Medical Center and is believed to be unharmed. It is unclear if Francis is related to the child. Francis has been charged with injury to a minor and reckless endangerment. She posted a $75,000 bond and is scheduled to appear in court on August 13. The incident occurred near Lena's Nails, where a passerby noticed the child and called 911.

article_content: A devastating fire broke out on Srinagar’s Dal Lake on Saturday, destroying five houseboats and damaging seven huts. Three Bangladeshi tourists, identified as Anindaya Kowshal, Das Gupta, and Mohammad Moinud—who were staying in the houseboat ‘Safeena’—tragically lost their lives. According to officials, one of the deceased is believed to be a woman. Rescue workers from the State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) recovered the bodies while clearing debris. DNA samples have been collected to confirm the victims’ identities. The fire is thought to have started in a single houseboat before quickly spreading to nearby houseboats. The precise cause of the fire remains unknown. Fire and emergency services, along with SDRF personnel, responded swiftly, evacuating several other tourists from adjacent houseboats. Senior officials, including Srinagar Deputy Commissioner Ajaz Asad, visited the scene to assess the situation. Travel operator records confirm the three who died were Bangladeshi tourists visiting the region. Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha expressed deep sorrow over the loss of life, offering his condolences and directing authorities to provide full assistance to those affected. Houseboats, made primarily of wood, are highly susceptible to fires. A similar incident occurred in April this year at Nageen Lake, where seven houseboats were destroyed. Although a full assessment is pending, officials estimate that the property damage from the Dal Lake fire runs into several crores of rupees. Houseboats are a major tourist attraction in Srinagar, typically valued between Rs 2-5 crore each.

Mburuvichakuéra he’i peteî tapicha omanóva kuña ikatuha. Estado Salvataje ha Respuesta Frente a Desastres (SDRF) rembiapokue ojuhu hetahápe umi hetave rembyre. Bombero kuéra ha SDRF atýra oho pya’épe, ha oipe’a hetave viajante ambue karumbe reheguágui. Mburuvicha guasu, Siringar Deputy Commissioner Ajaz Asad, oho avei ohecha mba’e ojehupyty. Jasypa-pe, Nageen Lake-pe, siete karumbe oñembyai tatay rehe. Ojekuaa gueteri mboy mba’e oñehundi hague, péro mburuvicha kuéra he’i heta millón rupiah mba’e oñehundi hague. article_content: On February 10, 2022, international media gathered at the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) as an armored car delivered a precious cargo: the world’s largest gold bracteate. Measuring 13.5 cm, this medallion-like necklace was discovered alongside 15 other bracteates and four Roman medallions the previous year by an amateur archaeologist near Vindelev, Denmark. Weighing a total of 794 grams, the gold hoard is thought to have been buried in the 6th century. Experts have likened its significance to Denmark’s famed Golden Horns of Gallehus. Many of the bracteates are so tightly folded that crucial motifs and runic inscriptions are hidden. Attempting to unfold the fragile gold by hand would risk destruction, prompting Denmark’s National Museum and the Vejle Museums to seek high-tech assistance at DTU’s 3D Imaging Center. Archaeologist and research head Mads Ravn explained, 'Sometimes technology can open doors we can’t. By revealing the images and inscriptions, we hope to learn more about the nobleman who once owned this treasure and gain insights into society’s structure in the 5th and 6th centuries.' DTU researchers employ CT scanning—commonly used in hospitals for internal imaging—to create thousands of detailed X-ray images, allowing the bracteates to be digitally reconstructed and 'unfolded.' This approach previously helped DTU scan and reconstruct a T. rex skull. For the Vindelev hoard, 9,600 CT images were generated. Yet, the varying thickness of the gold, especially where stamping and engraving made it thin, complicates matters by introducing visual artifacts into the scans. Senior Research Officer Carsten Gundlach noted that, while the method produces fairly accurate 3D reconstructions, the artifacts make it challenging for colleague Hans Martin Kjer to digitally 'unfold' the thinly folded gold. 'Tight folds make it hard to define the precise boundaries, and separating surfaces is tricky. Achieving a perfect, detailed unfolding remains difficult,' Kjer explained. However, the researchers have shifted focus to digitally unfolding and analyzing specific sections rather than entire pieces. Historically, Denmark in the bracteate era was dominated by clan leaders ruling distinct territories—often compared to organized groups like biker gangs or the Mafia. The size and quality of the Vindelev treasure suggest an unknown but powerful leader once resided there. Archaeologists see clear connections between the motifs of the Vindelev find and treasures previously discovered near Gudme, another major power center in historic Denmark. These similarities lead to theories of alliances and exchanges between clans, possibly through marriage. By examining motifs and stamps on the artifacts, especially the largest bracteate with its twin motif, researchers hope to trace their origins to specific goldsmiths or regional workshops, potentially confirming connections between Vindelev and Gudme. Some bracteates seem purposefully folded as offerings, while others may have been damaged long after burial. Advanced mathematical algorithms might help distinguish between intentional and accidental folding. Recent work has succeeded in digitally unfolding smaller, less-complicated sections, providing clearer details than attempts to unfold an entire bracteate at once. The method opens new avenues for reconstructing and analyzing such ancient objects. The project’s progress has been met with enthusiasm by museums, who anticipate further answers about Iron Age dynasties, power exchanges, and ritual practices. The next step is to tackle the largest, most complex motifs and continue collaboration across archaeology and technology fields. As Hans Martin Kjer concludes, 'There are always new challenges in research. The work is never truly finished.'
translated_content: Arakõi jasypateĩ 10, 2022-pe, hetave tembiapo momarandu ojegueru DTU-pe (Teknika Mbo’ehaovusu, Dinamarca) peteî auto mbarete rehe peteî mba’e rehegua iñimportante: yvoty sa’yju tuichavéva. Ko joya, 13,5 cm rehegua, ojeguerekóva 15 ambue bracteate ha irundy medallón romano ndive, ojuhukuaákuri peteî karai amateu Vindelev ypýpe, Dinamarca. Sa’yju joa oĩ 794 gramo, ha oñemohenda ojeñotỹhague siglo VI-pe. Aranduha kuéra he’i ohechakuaa ha’eha peteĩ mba’e juruguaúva ha’eve Gallehus Horns rehegua. Heta bracteate ojepysóva ha ndaikatúi ojehecha umi retrato ha inskripción rúnica. Oñemohendávo oñepysóva ha hesapymi ojapo, ojaporãve Tetãygua Museo ha Vejle Museo-kuéra ha oñejerure ayuda teknológiko DTU 3D Imaging Center-pe. Mads Ravn he’i: 'Teknología ikatu ohape joko heta hendáicha. Jahecha hag̃ua umi imagen ha inskripción rehegua, ikatu ñande jaikuaa mba’eve ohupyty arandupyhára rajy ha mba’eichaitépa oiko haguékuri tetãygua 5-ta ha 6-ta siglo-pe.' DTU arandukuéra oipuru CT scan, oñemomba’eguasúva pohanoha rehe internamente, ojapo haguã heta imágen detallada rehe, ikatu haguã omoheñói digitalmente ha 'omoñapĩ' bracteate-kuéra. Ko técnica oipytyvõma DTU-scanea ha omoheñói haguã T. rex akã aregua. Vindelev hoard rehe, ojapo 9.600 CT imagen. Upeichavérõ, sa’yju poguapy ha ojepirúva ojapo artefacto visual rehe umíva imágen rehegua. Carsten Gundlach omombe’u ha’eha procedimiento porãite ojapo haguã 3D rehegua ojapo haguã accuracy rehe, péro artefacto ome’ẽ avei Hans Martin Kjer-pe heta mba’e omoñapĩ hag̃ua py’aguýpe digital rehe umi umi bracteate ombotuicháva. 'Ojuhu peteĩ henondegua oipysóva hasyeterei. Upévare hasýta omoonde haguã’i detále rehegua,' he’i Kjer. Upeichavérõguáicha, họ kuéra oiporavo ojehecha hag̃ua avei mba’eporãitéma, ojapóvo parte rehegua. Historicamente, Dinamarca bracteate ára, oguerekova’ekue líder rehegua clan ndive, ojoguaiterei grupo ojapo mba’e vaihápe. Vindelev mba’e sa’yju tuicha ha porãite he’i peteî líder guasu oguerekova’ekue poder. Arandukuéra ohecha heta retrato ojoguáva Gudme rehegua, ambue poder rehegua Dinamarca. Ko’ã mba’e ojapo oñembojojávo alianza rehe clan-kuéra apytépe, ikatuha avei kasamiento rupive. Oñeha’arõ oñeikuaa umi retrato ha sello rehegua, tuichavéva, ojapo rupa umi joyero térã taller departamento rehegua. Oĩ bracteate oñepysóva ojapoháicha ofrénda rehegua, ha ambue oike mombyry rire. Matemática algoritmo pyahu ikatu oipytyvõ oikuaa hag̃ua omoñapĩ ryepyre. Ojehupyty peteĩ resultado oñeha’ãvo digitalmente umi parte michî rehe osêva porãite. Método pyahu ohechauka jeikutu oñondive mba’ekuaa rehe. Museo-kuéra oñemomba’e hetaite oñeha’ãva rehe, ohupytyse hetave mba’ekuaarã reko rehegua, poder ha ceremonial rehegua. Oguerekóva ome’ẽse umi retrato tuichavéva, oipytũ meme arandupyhára ha científica rehegua oñondive. Hans Martin Kjer omohu’ã he’i: 'Oĩ heta mba’e oñemomba’eva’erã. Jajoapy oñemohenda rire.'

article_content: Dr. Sharon T. McLaughlin-Weber, a New York-based plastic surgeon, founded Courage Couture—a lingerie brand devoted to women who have undergone mastectomy or reconstructive breast surgery. Motivated by her own reconstructive surgery following a lymphoma diagnosis at age 13, Dr. McLaughlin-Weber set out to create more inclusive options for survivors. Currently, Courage Couture offers two sleep bras and a bikini top, each meticulously designed to support prosthetic use, address surgical scars, and meet the needs specific to mastectomy recovery. The garments feature elastic, adjustable fabrics, allowing users to tailor the fit and decide how much cleavage to display, according to personal comfort and style. Dr. McLaughlin-Weber has expressed hope that one day, a model with a mastectomy will wear her bikini designs in major publications, showcasing that beauty and confidence are for everyone. Earlier this year, a petition gathered over 120,000 signatures urging Victoria's Secret to introduce lingerie for mastectomy patients. However, the company declined, citing design complexities—a decision Dr. McLaughlin-Weber questioned, given their substantial resources. Though she doesn't believe large brands are obligated to produce such lines, Dr. McLaughlin-Weber feels they should be motivated to do so. In lieu of their action, Courage Couture fills this need. The line’s items, priced at $85, also benefit women with uneven breasts, whether from surgery or birth. Above all, Courage Couture is about empowering women after mastectomy to feel just as sexy and self-assured as anyone else.

Ha’e ojapo ko tembiapo ha’e voi ohasa rire cirugía rekove, leukemia ogueraha va’ekue imitãme. Ko’ág̃a Courage Couture oguereko mokõi sujetador pyhare ha peteĩ bikini ári, ojapo haguéicha upeichaite ojokupyty prótesis rehe, ai rembyre ha ambue mba’e mastectomía rire oñeikotevẽva. Umi ao oguereko tela elástica ha ojokupyty hag̃ua kebutuhan rehe ha kuña ikatu ojapo cleavage ojehechauka, oipotahaicha. Dr. McLaughlin-Weber oha’arõ peteî ára peteî modelo mastectomía rehe orekóva omondéta bikini apopyre pe revista tuichapyrĩvape, ohechauka hag̃ua porã pe belleza ha jeroviapy opa kuñápe g̃uarã. Pe aro rire peteĩ petición omoañetete kuri 120.000 firma rupi Victoria’s Secret-ipe ojapo hag̃ua lingerie mastectomía rehe. Upéicharamo hikuái ndojapói, he’ígui ijetu’uha diseño. Dr. McLaughlin-Weber ndojerovíri ko’ã razón rehe, ohecha haguére oreko heta recurso. Ha’e he’i umi marka tuicháva ndorekói obligación, péro ojapo va’erãha ojapose mba’e porã. Umi marca guasu ndoikuaa’ývo, Courage Couture oñemomba’e. Ko línea, oñevende $85 rehe, avei oipytyvõ kuña oguerekóva teta ijafekiláva surgery térã genética rupive. Courage Couture oñeha’ã ombopy’aguasu opa kuña mastectomía rire oñandu hag̃ua ijerovia ha imba’eteetésa.

In Rivers State, Nigeria, police say two suspected members of a notorious cult were killed after attacking the Odiemerenyi community, where five residents lost their lives early Sunday. Police spokesperson Grace Iringe-Koko explained that officers responded to information that the suspects—associated with wanted gang leader David Gift, also called 2-Baba—were seeking out police informants. The same group is alleged to have murdered Divisional Police Officer SP Bako Angbanshin in September.

When police arrived, the suspects opened fire, resulting in a shootout. Two of the cultists were fatally wounded during the encounter. The state’s Commissioner of Police has directed officers to step up the hunt for 2-Baba and other fugitives to bring them to justice.

Police have reassured local residents that additional security measures are in place and offered their sympathies to the families affected by this violence.

Policía oñeʼẽva, Grace Iringe-Koko, omombeʼu oficial-kuéra ohoha pyaʼeterei orekógui marandu heʻihápe, umi ojekuhague suspect-kuéra, ojehesa David Gift rehegua, ojeikuaáva avei 2-Baba ramo, oheka hague informante policía rehegua. Ko grupo oñemohendáva avei omoakãha omoguevi haguã SP Bako Angbanshin, Divisional Police Officer, jasyporundy jave.

Oguahẽvo policía-kuéra, suspect-kuéra oapysa piroʼy hese, ha oñepyrũ oñorairõ hikuái. Mokõi cultista oñemohendu hetekue omano hague upe rire. Komisionado Policía omeʼẽ orden oñembohape hag̃ua tembiapo ojejapóva ojuhupa hag̃ua 2-Baba ha umi oĩva fuga-pe oñembojapo hag̃ua justicia.

article_content: Cruise holidays are becoming increasingly popular, and companies are finding innovative ways to accommodate more passengers. Rather than constructing entirely new vessels at significant expense, cruise lines like MSC Cruises are expanding their current ships by cutting them and adding new sections before reassembling them. Striking photographs highlight MSC Sinfonia's transformation at the Fincantieri shipyard in Palermo, Sicily. The process, reminiscent of a giant Lego set, involves splitting the ship and adding a new midsection. MSC Cruises has started this extensive renovation on MSC Sinfonia, the second of its four Lirica-class ships. The enlargement process requires cutting the ship in half, inserting a new extension, and 'sewing' it back together. Work proceeds around the clock to achieve the ambitious 10-week timeline. Although the construction process may seem complex, the final result is expected to be impressive. The refit includes dedicated kids’ club areas sponsored by well-known brands Lego and Chicco. These enhancements are part of the £150 million (€200 million) 'Renaissance project,' which installs 79-foot midsections on four ships. Fincantieri’s skilled marine engineers carefully separated MSC Sinfonia’s hull, drawing the two halves apart to insert a 2,200GT, 79-foot midsection containing 193 extra cabins. In addition to the extension, the interior refurbishment will bring more comfort and space for guests, an upgraded MSC Aurea Spa with extra massage areas, and a new outdoor spray park on deck 13. Preparations for the project started before the Sinfonia’s arrival, with the new midsection floated into the dry dock on January 9. The vessel will remain there throughout the transformation and sea trials. Once complete, the larger and enhanced MSC Sinfonia will leave the shipyard on March 25 for Genoa and begin its maiden voyage to Ajaccio, Barcelona, and Marseille. Giles Hawke, MSC Cruises executive director for the UK and Ireland, expressed enthusiasm for the expanded family offerings and celebrated the partnerships with Lego and Chicco. MSC Cruises currently accommodates about 40,000 guests daily. Following the completion of the Renaissance Programme and delivery of the seventh planned ship by 2022, the company anticipates doubling daily capacity to 80,000 guests, or 3.4 million annually.

article_content: NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter captured images of the Curiosity rover making its way across the Martian terrain towards Mount Sharp. The orbiter’s HiRISE camera photographed these scenes on December 11, 2013, showing Curiosity navigating around obstacles and leaving tracks on the planet’s surface. The rover appears in the lower left of the images, with wheel tracks roughly three meters (ten feet) apart marking its route. HiRISE had previously imaged Curiosity’s landing 17 months earlier and has since monitored the rover’s movements from orbit. One detailed image focuses on the rover’s tracks over rugged ground, documenting the journey between October and December 2013. Other visuals combine orbital views with ‘rover’s-eye’ snapshots at selected spots, captured by Curiosity’s onboard cameras. Mount Sharp, also known as Aeolis Mons, rises over five kilometers (three miles) from the center of Gale Crater. Its layered geology offers scientists vital clues about how Mars’ environment has changed over time. Curiosity’s mission is to investigate Mars’ potential to support life, a goal advanced by the discovery of an ancient, habitable environment at Yellowknife Bay following the rover’s 2012 landing. After departing Yellowknife Bay in July 2013, Curiosity has traveled about 8.6 kilometers (5.3 miles) towards Mount Sharp’s foothills, aiming to arrive there by mid-2014. The collected orbital and rover images together provide a comprehensive view of the rover’s ongoing exploration and forthcoming scientific challenges on Mars.

Rover ojehecha ima'e'ỹ ijykévo ta'angápe, hasa reheve mba'éichapa roda rapére oĩ mbohapy metro (10 píe) ári. Peteĩ ta'ãnga tuichavéva ohechauka Curiosity raperea yvy atýpe, oikundaha rire octubre guive diciembre 2013 peve. Oĩ avei ambue ta'angami orbital rehegua ha ‘ohecha rover’ rehegua, oñemboja umi tenda ojeiporavo haguépe, Curiosity rembiaporã guive. Mount Sharp, hérava avei Aeolis Mons, opu’ã 5 kilometro (3 milla) rupi Gale Crater mbytépe. I apakua apañuãi rehegua oroguatáva heta mba’e oikuaaukáva Mars rembiasakue rehe. Curiosity rembiapo hína oikuaa haguã Mars ikatupa kuri ombopyahu tekove, ha upéicha ojuhúma peteĩ tenda ymaiteguare ikatúva gueteri oiko tekove Yellowknife Bay-pe, oguejy rire 2012-pe. Upe rire, oheja Yellowknife Bay julio 2013-pe guive, Curiosity oikotevẽ 8,6 kilometro (5,3 milla) ova haguã Mount Sharp yvykuáre gotyo, ha og̃uahẽtaha upépe ary 2014 mbytépe. Ko’ã ta'angakuéra rehegua oikuaauka porã mba’éichapa táva rover oike ha umi mba’e pyahu Mars rehegua ojehupytyse.

article_content: For the first time ever, three drones soared up to 1,000 feet above Sydney's Harbour Bridge, Opera House, and the water barges, capturing exclusive 360-degree high-definition footage of the New Year's Eve fireworks display. Each drone was equipped with six HD cameras, providing unique aerial perspectives of the dazzling pyrotechnics. This innovative footage was broadcast live across ABC's coverage and streamed on Telstra's YouTube channel, allowing viewers around the world to experience the event as never before. Sydney Lord Mayor Clover Moore expressed excitement over the broadcast's anticipated reach, stating that the images would be seen by a billion people globally. Mayor Moore encouraged those celebrating at home to tune in for the event, highlighting the inclusion of never-before-seen drone visuals. She also announced another technological first: tweets using the hashtag #SydNYE were projected onto the Harbour Bridge in real time. The use of drones and live tweet projections marked a milestone for Sydney's New Year's Eve celebrations. The city saw massive crowds, with more than 1.6 million Sydneysiders filling the Harbour area. Key vantage points like Mrs Macquarie's Point, the Tarpeian Precinct, the Sydney Opera House, and Mary Booth were closed once they reached capacity, as reported by The Australian. The festivities included 50 vessels carrying more than 8,000 people, lighting up the Harbour after the first round of fireworks at 9 p.m., as thousands gathered to welcome the New Year.

Peteĩ-teĩ drone oguereko poteĩ cámara HD, ome’ẽvo ángulo aéreo hechaukáva mba’éichapa ojajehecha umi fuegos artificiales. Ko video pyahu ojehechauka ABC retransmisión-pe ha avei Telstra YouTube canal rehe, ombohasávo ko aty guasu opáichavo, maymáva ohecha hag̃ua experiéncia pyahu. Dron ha tweet proyectado ohechauka innovación tuicháva Ary Pyahu pyhare ojehecháva Sydney-pe. Upépe ojehecha aty guasu, mas de 1.6 millón Sydneysider oĩ Harbour-pe. Vantage point herakuãvéva, Mrs Macquarie’s Point, Tarpeian Precinct, Sydney Opera House ha Mary Booth, oñemboty hokuévo ohenonde’a, he’i The Australian. Ko fiesta avei oguereko 50 barco, ogueraha 8.000 tapicha rupi, ha ohesape Harbour upe rire umi fuegos artificiales primera ronda 9 p.m-pe, heta tapicha oñembyatýva ohasárõ Ary Pyahu pyhare.

article_content: Over nine months ago, Uber suffered a security breach that may have revealed the names and driver's license numbers of around 50,000 drivers across different U.S. states, the company has disclosed. Katherine Tassi, Uber’s data privacy counsel, wrote on the company’s blog that both current and past drivers might be affected. Uber has informed authorities in states where drivers are impacted, including California. So far, there is no sign that the leaked information has been misused. The breach actually took place in May 2014, but wasn’t discovered until September that year. After its discovery, Uber strengthened its database security and began investigating the incident. A company spokesperson told the New York Post that Uber delayed announcing the breach for more than five months due to the ongoing investigation, refusing to give further explanation. Cybersecurity expert Michael Kroll from Kroll told the Los Angeles Times that names and driver’s license numbers alone are typically not enough for identity theft, but could be problematic if paired with more personal information. Out of all the drivers affected, about 21,000 are based in California, according to the LA Times. Uber said the breach was a single unauthorized access by a third party. On the day it announced the breach, Uber filed a lawsuit in federal court in San Francisco against an unknown hacker, hoping the legal process will help identify the responsible person. Affected drivers have been advised to watch their credit reports for suspicious activity, and Uber is offering them a free year of identity protection. Uber’s approach to user data has faced criticism before, with allegations that employees improperly accessed customer information. The company is also dealing with lawsuits and protests in India, where there are calls to ban its service. Valued at $40 billion and backed by major investors like Benchmark and Google Ventures, Uber is the most valuable startup in the country.

Katherine Tassi, Uber peguare ohupyty hag̃ua protección datos rehegua, he’i blog-pe chófer kuéra ikatu oñeafecta. Uber omombe’u umi estado-pe chófer-kuéra oîva, California avei. Peteî portavoz he’i New York Post-pe ohechauka haguã cinco jasy rupi oñemombe’u haĝua, oîhaguéicha investigación, ha he’i avei ndaikatúi ome’ê hetave información. Kroll-gui Michael Kroll, especialista seguridad rehegua, he’i Los Angeles Times-pe réra ha chapa número ha’ente ndaha’éi suficiente identidad robarã, péro oñembojoajúramo ambue mba’erehe, ikatu ojeapo. Chóferkuérape oñemoñe’ẽ omaña haguã i crédito reporte rehe ha Uber ome’ẽ peteĩ año protección identidad rehe. article_content: A new California law, Assembly Bill 418, will ban certain food additives beginning in 2027. It's been popularly called the 'Skittles ban,' but Skittles will remain available since it’s not affected by the new restrictions. The law focuses on specific ingredients linked to health concerns—like hyperactivity, nervous system issues, and cancer—that have long been prohibited in Europe. Titanium dioxide, once included in earlier drafts of the bill and used in Skittles, was ultimately excluded from the list of banned substances. However, products such as some flavors of PEZ and Peeps (which include Red 3), and Sun Drop soda (containing brominated vegetable oil), will need to adjust their recipes to comply. Given California's influence, these changes are likely to extend beyond the state as companies find it more practical to update recipes nationwide. Governor Gavin Newsom, who signed the bill, highlighted that prohibiting these additives brings California in line with international safety standards. Companies have until 2027 to modify their ingredients and will likely adapt existing products rather than withdraw them from California stores. As evidence, Skittles continues to be sold in Europe under similar additive bans.

article_content: Taking a photo on your next bushwalk could help predict and prevent devastating bushfires, thanks to NOBURN, a new mobile phone app powered by artificial intelligence developed by University of Adelaide experts. "The app’s AI computer vision can analyze photos submitted by users in fire-prone areas to assess potential bushfire fuel loads," said Professor Javen Shi, Director of Advanced Reasoning and Learning at the University's Australian Institute for Machine Learning (AIML). "This data is used to estimate the severity of a potential bushfire and how far it might spread." According to Professor Shi, the AI models for the app mimic the judgment of human experts who usually scour bushland for fire hazards. "Once the model is trained, we won’t need experts to visit every forest," said Professor Shi. "We could have thousands of citizens—such as bushwalkers and campers—taking photos our AI can use to make predictions." Gathering quality data from NOBURN users could take up to 12 months, with another year required to train the app’s AI using images from rural areas. Professor Shi explains that the app's main goal is to raise awareness of how investment in AI can help prevent the destructive impacts of bushfires. "The app itself is just a start, but we hope this will excite the public and foster hope, as we lose millions of dollars each year to bushfires," Professor Shi said. "We aim to expand this into a situational awareness tool, like a command center for bushfire commanders. They would be able to see in real time how resources are deployed and how fires are spreading, and we can build AI to support them." "We also envision an AI assistant that can converse with commanders and firefighters—much like Iron Man’s AI—to provide real-time advice and improve situational awareness in low visibility." The app idea emerged after the 2019-2020 Black Summer bushfires, which burned more than 46 million acres, destroyed over 9,000 properties, claimed 34 lives, and cost farmers up to $7 billion in damages. Professor Shi collaborated with University of the Sunshine Coast forestry experts Dr. Sam Van Holsbeeck and Professor Mark Brown, as well as Professor Paul Salmon, Director of the Center for Human Factors and Sociotechnical Systems, to develop NOBURN. "AI has vast potential to lead in assessing fuel hazards and bushfire prediction and simulation, as we are exploring with AIML," said Dr. Van Holsbeeck. "This isn’t just a bushfire research project; it’s a collaboration across disciplines that makes bushfire research accessible to everyone."

article_content: San Diego (CNN) -- The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is currently experiencing internal conflict. Recently, two unions representing nearly 20,000 DHS employees joined together to publicly oppose the Senate immigration reform bill introduced by the so-called 'Gang of Eight.' The coalition includes 12,000 employees who issue documents granting some immigrants legal status in the United States and 7,700 agents responsible for deporting those in the country illegally. The unions claim the bill could compromise public safety. Complicating matters, President Barack Obama and Homeland Security Secretary Janet Napolitano have both expressed support for the Senate's immigration reform. Obama emphasizes the importance of including a pathway to citizenship in any reform proposal, and White House press secretary Jay Carney noted that White House staff had collaborated with the eight senators involved in drafting the legislation. Many DHS employees opposed to the bill would still be tasked with carrying out its provisions if it becomes law, such as reviewing applications from undocumented immigrants seeking legal status or deporting those who do not qualify. How this will work in practice remains unclear. DHS unions have resisted policy changes before. In June 2011, ICE Director John Morton issued an internal memorandum, known as the 'Morton memo,' advising agents that they may use discretion and consider factors such as length of U.S. residency, age of arrival, and educational pursuit when making decisions about deportation. Many immigration reform advocates welcomed the memo as progress. However, according to immigration attorneys, some field agents ignored the guidance. As a result, high deportation rates continued, meeting the administration's enforcement goals. These numbers enabled the administration to present itself to Congress and the public as strict on immigration. In October 2011, just months after the Morton memo, Napolitano gave a speech at American University highlighting DHS’s record-setting deportation figures for fiscal year 2011, a record that was surpassed in 2012. By the end of 2013, the administration was projected to have deported 2 million people. Chris Crane, head of the National ICE Council, has criticized the administration’s enforcement record, telling The New York Times that the department is avoiding interior arrests. Critics, however, point to families affected by deportation—such as ten-year-old Stephanie Pucheta, who will spend Father's Day without her father, Julio Cesar Pucheta, who was deported earlier this year. In a testimonial for the advocacy group Cuentame, Stephanie described the emotional impact of her father's removal, saying she misses him daily and questioning why families must be separated. The administration has faced criticism for the hardship its deportation policies cause immigrant families, while presenting itself as firm on enforcement. The author questions whether the administration is being fully candid about its approach. This commentary expresses the opinions of Ruben Navarrette.

article_content: London’s Metropolitan Police have launched an investigation into the deaths of three young boys, a case involving claims of long-running organized sexual abuse. Operation Midland, which began last month, is focusing on abuse reported from more than 30 years ago. Detectives are seeking help from the public—especially men who may have been abused as boys—for any information that can help identify victims, witnesses, or abusers. Detective Superintendent Kenny McDonald called on other potential survivors to come forward, expressing his belief that further victims may be out there, or people who witnessed the abuse. The team is also examining whether these abuse cases might be linked to the suspected murders of the three boys. Police have not yet found any bodies, but are reviewing missing persons reports from that era. Investigators say the abuse lasted at least a decade and occurred across various locations in London and nearby counties, including at some military sites. Dolphin Square, an apartment complex in Pimlico, has been cited as one location involved. A witness named 'Nick' claims he was abused from ages seven to sixteen, between 1975 and 1984. He says he was taken by car to the Dolphin Square apartment, where abuse took place by individuals, groups, and during parties. Police are appealing to anyone who lived in the area since the early 1970s and may have noticed anything suspicious, as their recollections could help the investigation. Officers are in touch with the relatives of two boys—one who disappeared in 1979 and another who disappeared and was later found murdered in 1981—but it remains uncertain if these cases are connected.

article_content: The autumn/winter 2015 menswear season showcases bold and innovative styles, especially at London Collections: Men. Christopher Shannon, a young designer from Liverpool and Central Saint Martins graduate, debuted a stand-out collection featuring statement jumpers with sombre slogans like 'Broke', 'Broken', 'Save Me', and 'Thanks 4 Nothing'. Notably, male models wore plastic carrier bags as headgear or face coverings, fashioned by co-stylist Judy Blame into hats, jewelry, or masks with eye holes. Shannon’s designs combined sportswear elements such as chunky work boots and sheer or slashed trousers with surprising accents like tutu belts and peplums inspired by boxer short waistbands, offering a fresh take on streetwear.  The knitwear label Sibling made a vibrant impression with a pink and punk-inspired collection including striped jumpers, scarves, and onesies crafted from candy-colored yarns. Their runway featured models with painted hair carrying giant teddy bears, wearing everything from neatly tailored knits to intentionally distressed, cobweb-like jumpers—emphasizing Sibling’s playful design ethos.  Fashion East, a non-profit initiative which champions emerging designers, brought Roaring Twenties flair with beaded headdresses, finger waves, diamond necklaces, and plush velvet suits paired with ballet pumps. Their collection included modern pinstriped ensembles, like sleeveless crop tops and shorts or asymmetrical tops with ripped skinnies, often styled with Nike sneakers. Fashion East continues to support innovative designers, encouraging new approaches to androgynous fashion.  London Collections: Men, the male counterpart to London Fashion Week, emphasizes British menswear’s creativity and commercial value. The event features notable brands including Barbour, Burberry, Belstaff, and Tom Ford, spanning key venues like the Hospital Club and Victoria House. Its program shines a spotlight on both global brands and emerging talent, displaying the breadth of British fashion ingenuity.

article_content: Julie Bentley, the chief executive of Girl Guiding UK, is determined to shed the organization’s ‘middle-class’ image and encourage more young people from diverse backgrounds to join. She believes Girl Guiding UK is much 'cooler' than many realize and is working to show young people what being a Girl Guide is truly like. While Bentley is committed to modernizing the organization’s image, she also wants to preserve its valued traditions—such as making chocolate and building campfires. Having grown up in a working-class background, Bentley herself once thought the Girl Guides was only for middle-class girls, but now she emphasizes that the organization reflects the diversity of its local communities. Bentley admits that Girl Guiding UK has an image problem and is determined to improve public perception. 'I haven’t made Guides cool. I’ve just shown everyone how cool it is,' she told the Daily Telegraph. She acknowledges a disconnect between what Girl Guiding UK actually offers and what people assume about it, and is striving to highlight the reality that it welcomes everyone. The organization is working closely with charities and youth workers to engage girls in deprived communities and set up new units in areas where there previously weren’t any. The Duchess of Cambridge, who is a former Girl Guide, actively supports the Girl Guiding and Scouting movements. Membership numbers have grown steadily over the past several years, with 546,406 members and supporters across all age groups, from girls as young as five to young women up to 26. However, there are waiting lists in many regions, and to continue expanding, the organization needs more volunteers from a wide range of backgrounds to lead local programs. Bentley has described Girl Guiding UK as the ‘ultimate feminist organization’ because it equips girls with confidence and vital life skills. She emphasizes the need to help girls overcome barriers and is eager for the organization to be recognized as both fun and appealing to young people.

article_content: Doctor Who has received criticism for a scene featuring Peter Capaldi and Jenna Coleman pulling out hair, which some viewers found distressing, particularly those suffering from trichotillomania—a disorder characterized by compulsive hair pulling. The scene, appearing in the first episode of series eight, showed the Doctor (Capaldi) pulling out a strand of his own hair before pulling a strand from Clara Oswald (Coleman), causing discomfort for her character. This sequence prompted complaints on social media, with viewers and trichotillomania sufferers describing the moment as 'insensitive' and 'triggering'. Trichotillomania is a psychological impulse-control disorder where an individual feels compelled to pull out their hair, leading to anxiety and, for some, significant emotional distress. There is currently no known cure. Rebecca Brown, a prominent vlogger from Essex who documents her experience with trichotillomania on YouTube, was among those who spoke out. She described feeling 'unprepared' for the content and noted that the unexpected depiction made it difficult for her to avoid being triggered. In her video response, she expressed frustration with the lack of understanding about the condition and the mixed reactions from the Doctor Who fandom. On Twitter, viewers echoed these concerns, saying the scene could exacerbate struggles for those with trichotillomania. Support group @LetsBeatTrich also warned viewers about potential triggers contained in the episode. An estimated one million people in the UK suffer from trichotillomania, most of them women. BBC representatives declined to comment on the controversy.

Pe escena ojehechámi primera episodio serie ocho-pe, upépe Doctor (Capaldi) ojokuávo peteî hague ijarehegui ha upéi ojokuávo Clara Oswald (Coleman) rehe, omoñembyai haguã chupe. Nigeria is evaluating the option of joining BRICS within the next two years. Foreign Affairs Minister Yusuf Tuggar has stated that affiliations will only be pursued if they match Nigeria’s objectives and offer transparent intentions. Tuggar emphasized Nigeria’s position as a significant nation prepared to choose its global partners wisely.

The government insists that joining groups like BRICS or the G-20 will hinge on clear benefits to Nigeria, with the country’s large population and economy supporting its suitability for these alliances. BRICS currently includes Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa, and recently invited Saudi Arabia, Iran, Egypt, Argentina, Ethiopia, and the UAE to join.

Addressing public speculation, officials have reiterated that Nigeria hasn’t applied for membership in either BRICS or the G-20. Vice President Kashim Shettima mentioned that decisions will only be made after consulting advisory and legislative bodies, in line with President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s consensus-driven approach.

Special Adviser Ajuri Ngelale added that detailed risk and benefit assessments are underway within the government. Authorities stress that any decision will be based on thorough, evidence-based analysis, ensuring that Nigeria’s national interest and economic welfare are prioritized. Analysts suggest that if Nigeria were to join BRICS, it could gain significant economic and international advantages.

article_content: Bill Clinton, former U.S. President, and his wife, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, have a net worth estimated between $10 million and $50 million, according to financial disclosures. Despite this, taxpayers provide nearly $1 million each year for their post-White House expenses. Like the other living former presidents—Jimmy Carter and George W. Bush—Clinton receives a $201,000 annual pension. In 2014, the Clintons’ publicly funded expenses included $157,000 for staff salaries and benefits, $414,000 for office space in Harlem, New York, and $9,000 for phone bills. Bill Clinton’s total post-presidential support reached about $944,000 that year, according to The Washington Post. George W. Bush's taxpayer-funded expenses in 2014 were higher, totaling $1.28 million, as reported by the Congressional Research Service. His expenses included $102,000 for phone services and $135,000 for office furniture, computers, and supplies. By comparison, Jimmy Carter's office space cost $109,000, and his total expenses were $466,000. These ongoing government funds have sparked debate over whether wealthy former presidents should continue to receive such support. In 2012, Representative Jason Chaffetz introduced the Presidential Allowance Modernization Act, aiming to cap government spending on former presidents at $400,000 per year, reduced by any personal earnings, but the bill did not pass. Public discussion intensified after Hillary Clinton commented in a June 9 ABC News interview that she and Bill were 'dead broke' after leaving the White House, referencing costs like mortgages and their daughter Chelsea’s education. Bill Clinton defended their circumstances, suggesting that focusing on their wealth is not the main issue. He instead emphasized broader economic struggles affecting Americans. At a Clinton Global Initiative event in Denver ahead of the 2016 election, the Clintons presented themselves as advocates for the middle class and the underprivileged. Hillary highlighted the importance of community in upward mobility. She has not announced a decision on running for president. The Former Presidents Act of 1958 provides former presidents with pensions, office allowances, staff, medical coverage, and lifelong Secret Service protection. The law aims to prevent financial hardship in retirement, though some critics argue that modern former presidents are financially secure from activities like book deals and speaking events. Jimmy Carter, who left office in 1981, receives the least government support among living former presidents, with annual expenses much lower than those of Clinton or Bush.

The BBC’s effort to relaunch the renowned period drama 'Upstairs Downstairs' in competition with ITV's popular ‘Downton Abbey’ has come to a close after two series. Despite significant investment in sets, costumes, and featuring acclaimed performers such as Keeley Hawes, Ed Stoppard, and Claire Foy, the revival struggled to maintain its viewership.

To try to boost ratings, new characters were added and sensational storylines introduced—such as Dr Blanche Mottershead’s (Alex Kingston) romantic involvement with Emilia Fox’s character—but these additions were met with criticism and failed to halt the decline in popularity.

Launching with 6.5 million viewers in 2010, the show saw audience numbers drop to 4.45 million by the end of its second series. In contrast, ‘Downton Abbey’ attracted 10.5 million viewers for its second series finale.

Dame Eileen Atkins and Jean Marsh, who created the original 1971 series, were involved in the new version, which is set during the years leading up to World War II at 165 Eaton Place. However, the production was hampered by Atkins’ departure due to creative differences and Marsh’s reduced role following a minor stroke. The cast also included Art Malik and Anne Reid.

Despite high hopes and a talented team, the program failed to reach its intended success. The BBC reported there are currently no plans for another series. Dame Eileen Atkins expressed regret at the cancellation and commended the commitment of the cast.

Jeporu heta viru ha tapicha arandupy oku’éva, umíva apytépe Keeley Hawes, Ed Stoppard ha Claire Foy, ndikatúi ohechauka upe ojehupytyse va’ekue umi ohecháva rehe.

Ojehupytyse hag̃ua ohechávo tapicha, omoinge umi personaje pyahu ha omotenonde mombe’ugua’ukuéra ojepotáva—Dr. Blanche Mottershead (Alex Kingston) rembiapokue avei ohayhu Emilia Fox rehe—péro upéva ndovalei ni peteĩ ha umi ohecháva ikatupyryete oñembohape, he’ívo ndaha’éi ha’eháicha tape porã.

Oñepyrũvo 2010-pe 6,5 millón ohecháva, ha mokõihá temporada paha osẽ 4,45 millón che rehe. ‘Downton Abbey’ katu ojapo 10,5 millón ohechapaitépe mokõihá temporada paha.

Dame Eileen Atkins ha Jean Marsh, umi ohapejokokuaáva primera serie 1971-pe, ojepytaso ko versión pyahúpe avei, oikohápe 165 Eaton Place-pe Londres-pe, ojeprepara ohupyty hag̃ua Guerra Mundial II rembiapo. Jepémo upéicha, oike hikuái apañuái guasuhápe: Atkins osẽ ndovy’okuaái productor-kuéra rembiapóre, ha Marsh omboguejy iñemomba’e peteĩ raséma rire. Art Malik ha Anne Reid avei oĩ umi tapicha porã rehe.

Ojejapo heta jepy’a guasu ha tapicha katupyry reheve, añetehápe pe programa ndohupytyi upe ojehupytyse va’ekue. BBC ohechauka ko’ag̃aite peve ndaipóri plan ojapo jey hag̃ua ambue serie. Dame Eileen Atkins ohechauka oñembyasy, ha omomba’e umi actore rembiapo mbytetépe.

article_content: The Google Pixel 8 and Pixel 8 Pro were widely leaked ahead of their official launch, but excitement remains high for Google’s latest smartphones. These devices are among the most advanced offerings from Google to date.  The Pixel 8 lineup debuts the Google Tensor G3 processor, offers a variable 120Hz refresh rate on both models, and includes up to 1TB of storage on the Pro version. While both phones are top-tier, the Pro model is clearly positioned as the more premium device.  Design changes are subtle compared to the Pixel 7 series. Both phones retain rounded corners, a glass-over-metal build, and the signature camera visor. The Pro is larger and heavier, weighing over 200 grams.  Both phones feature variable 120Hz displays, but the Pro can reduce its refresh rate all the way down to 1Hz, enhancing battery life. The Pixel 8’s display reaches a minimum of 60Hz. Both are brighter than previous models, though the Pro boasts higher peak brightness.  Regarding durability, both phones have an IP68 rating for water and dust resistance. The Pro uses Gorilla Glass Victus 2, while the standard Pixel 8 uses the original Victus version. Both are built to withstand daily wear.  Performance is largely equal, thanks to the new Tensor G3 chip in both devices. Storage is more flexible on the Pro, offering 512GB and 1TB options in addition to 128GB and 256GB. The Pixel 8 is limited to 128GB or 256GB.  Battery life is expected to be similar, though the Pro has a larger battery and screen. Both are advertised with up to 24 hours of typical use or 72 hours on Extreme Battery Saver. Charging speeds are slightly higher for the Pro, but the difference is marginal.  Camera capabilities distinguish the Pro model, featuring a 48MP telephoto lens with 5x periscope zoom and a 48MP ultrawide lens. The Pixel 8 also performs well, offering a 50MP main lens and 12MP ultrawide lens, but lacks the Pro’s advanced telephoto feature.  Both phones ship with Android 14 and promise seven years of operating system updates, offering an exceptionally long software support window for Android devices.  Special features focus on AI and machine learning. Magic Eraser has been improved, and a new Best Take feature allows users to combine the best elements from multiple photos. Most features are shared across both phones, though only the Pro includes advanced manual camera controls.  The phones are available for preorder and release on October 12. The Pixel 8 starts at $699, while the Pixel 8 Pro starts at $999—both $100 more than their previous generation counterparts.  While the Pixel 8 Pro offers superior display and camera features, the $300 price gap is significant. The Pixel 8 remains a strong option, sharing many of the Pro’s core benefits at a lower price. Ultimately, the choice depends on whether users value the Pro’s extra features enough to justify the higher cost.

article_content: London's famous Trafalgar Square fountains have been switched off this summer because of new hosepipe restrictions introduced to combat severe water shortages. Thames Water ordered the shutdown as part of a broader ban aimed at saving water following two exceptionally dry winters. Ornamental fountains, including those at major tourist sites, are included in the restrictions. Current water reserves that supply the fountains are projected to be depleted by the weekend, according to the Greater London Authority. City officials are currently discussing whether a temporary solution can be found, especially since millions of tourists are expected to visit Trafalgar Square with the arrival of the Olympic Games and Jubilee celebrations. The newly enforced hosepipe ban impacts 20 million people across southern and eastern England. It prohibits using hoses and sprinklers for gardens, washing vehicles and boats, or for recreation. Watering cans are still allowed, and exceptions remain for those with blue badges and situations where cleaning is necessary for safety. Recent weather data shows rainfall levels well below the historical averages, with only 37% of the usual March rainfall recorded this year across England and Wales. February also saw an unusually low 46%. Due to the accumulated drought, water suppliers warn the hosepipe ban might stay in place into the autumn or even next year. Even if rainfall returns to normal, much of it will be soaked up by dry soil and plants, offering little relief. Some rivers and reservoirs, such as the River Kennet near Marlborough and areas including Shropshire, the Chilterns, and the North Downs, are reported to be at historic low levels. In previous years, similar bans have lasted many months—the 2005 South East ban continued for more than a year. Controversy has arisen over reports of significant water company leaks and recent executive payouts. Last year alone, companies lost enough water daily to supply 20 million people. Leaders in these companies reportedly received £4 million in bonuses in 2010-11, despite failing to meet leakage targets and distributing a £500 million windfall to mainly overseas shareholders after the drought was declared. Households are also facing financial pressure, with water bills increasing an average of 5.7%—even higher for some customers—just as the shortage bites. On a positive note, conservation groups like the RSPB support the restrictions, saying reduced demand will help protect river ecosystems and wildlife by keeping more water in the environment.

article_content: A second former employee has come forward alleging mistreatment by a wealthy New York City couple, following a lawsuit filed by their Chilean nanny over poor working conditions and inadequate pay. Malu Custer Edwards, 28, and Micky Hurley, 35, initially faced accusations from their nanny, Felicitas del Carmen Villanueva Garnica, who claims she was paid just $2 an hour for 12-hour workdays in their Upper East Side apartment. The latest complaint comes from photographer Roque Rodriguez, who says he was not paid $240 for photography work he did for the family in 2009. Instead, he received offensive and elitist emails from Hurley. In these emails, Hurley allegedly insulted Rodriguez and emphasized class differences between them. Rodriguez had requested payment for his work before providing images for a magazine spread, which led to Hurley sending derogatory and threatening correspondence. These reports surfaced after public scrutiny from the nanny’s lawsuit. Villanueva alleges she was required to work long hours, endured poor treatment, and was brought to the U.S. under false pretenses, including the use of a false passport. Villanueva claims that despite promises of $10 per hour and health benefits, she was paid only $800 a month, had minimal time off, and was not allowed to refill medication. She described her experience as 'forced labor' and 'involuntary servitude.' She stated that she was often given only bread and milk to eat, while the couple frequently dined at upscale restaurants. Villanueva eventually left in March 2011 after an alleged incident involving one of the children. The couple denies Villanueva's allegations and is contesting the lawsuit. However, the New York Department of Labor ordered Edwards and Hurley to pay Villanueva $6,302 in back wages in 2011.

article_content: Facebook is piloting a new payment system that may rival PayPal by allowing users to make mobile purchases using their Facebook login details. The feature aims to simplify online shopping by autofilling payment information already saved to users’ Facebook accounts, so customers don't need to repeatedly enter credit card data when buying via mobile apps. This pilot involves a partnership with the men's shopping site Jackthreads. Should the trial prove successful, Facebook could potentially compete directly with PayPal. Facebook has said it won’t process payments itself; instead, existing payment providers used by retail apps will keep handling the transactions. One key goal of the initiative is to enhance the checkout process for mobile users. Experts suggest that, if adopted more widely, the system could give Facebook valuable insights into shopping habits—information useful for targeted advertising. Facebook recently announced it is discontinuing its 'Credits' virtual currency in favor of local currency payments. This transition is intended to make purchases easier for users across the globe and simplify pricing for developers. The earlier Credits system, launched in 2009, became less necessary as most games moved to their own in-game currencies. However, privacy concerns remain. Critics wonder if users will trust Facebook with their financial data, especially after ongoing debates about privacy and features like Graph Search, which some users feel exposes personal information that was previously less accessible. Security is also an issue, since many smartphone owners do not use PINs or passwords to lock their devices. On the business side, Facebook reported second-quarter revenue of $1.813 billion—a 53% increase over the previous year—and $333 million in net income. User activity is rising, with 699 million daily active users in June and monthly mobile users up 51% to 819 million. Despite an initial period of poor stock performance after its 2012 IPO, Facebook's share price recently jumped 20% following strong financial results.

article_content: A civilian crew reportedly caused damage to the HMAS Canberra, a 27,000-tonne warship valued at $1.5 billion, during its initial 'shakedown cruise' between Sydney and Melbourne, according to media reports. The ship’s hull sustained minor damage and its electrical systems malfunctioned due to user error. The incidents occurred during a test voyage, where the civilian crew from Teekay Shipping Corporation operated the ship. According to The Daily Telegraph, the crew made two errors: operating the ship's electric pods at low-speed mode while traveling at high speed, causing vibrations throughout the vessel, and failing to disconnect emergency power, which led to an electrical melt-down, loss of steering, and the need to drop anchor for four hours. The vibrations caused some paint to peel from the hull, but overall damage was minimal. Both issues occurred during the ship’s first test cruise in May. A source quoted in The Daily Telegraph emphasized that these were not due to design flaws, but operator mistakes. Teekay Shipping Australia, which provided the crew, disputed these claims, stating that the reported incidents were 'fallacious' and that their staff were not negligent. Other issues discovered during the cruise included corrosion on propeller nuts and a small hull crack, attributed to the long barge journey from Spain, where the vessel was built. The HMAS Canberra is the first of two Landing Helicopter Docks being constructed for the Royal Australian Navy, with the HMAS Adelaide still being outfitted. These will be the largest ships in the Navy’s history and are expected to be based in Townsville, Queensland. The Canberra is expected to be commissioned later this year. Specifications: Length – 230.82 meters; Displacement – 27,500 tonnes; Speed – up to 20 knots; Capacity – up to 110 vehicles and 1,600 troops; Cost – $1.5 billion each. The article also outlines other vessels in the Royal Australian Navy, including guided missile frigates, patrol boats, minehunters, landing craft, surveying ships, support ships, submarines, and miscellaneous craft, with the numbers and functions of each described.

article_content: From first smiles to first teeth, baby steps, and heading off to school, it’s common for parents to capture precious moments of their children's lives. But Suman Bansal, from Gillingham, Kent, has been photographed every single day since she was born on May 16, 1996 — totaling an incredible 6,575 pictures. Suman, who turns 18 tomorrow, has grown up smiling for the camera, with her father Munish documenting her life from the very start. Now, every single photo has been brought together to form a giant portrait in time for her 18th birthday. The collection begins with Suman's ultrasound image from January 3, 1996, followed by photos chronicling each day of her life up to now. Munish, a 41-year-old accountant, began taking photographs of his wife Rita's ultrasound scans in January 1996. Since then, he has captured Suman's growth from baby to toddler, schoolgirl, and college student. "I decided to do this when Rita was pregnant," Munish explains. "I wanted to create a memory to see how our children changed day by day. It's amazing how much you can see when you look at daily photos." He mostly took pictures in the morning before school, but sometimes in the afternoon when the family returned home. "At first it was a real challenge, but it gradually became a routine. It’s a big commitment," he says. Only a couple of times did Munish nearly miss a day — once when he had to go to Suman’s aunt's house to take a photo, and another time when he almost forgot and had to wake the children. Suman’s brother Jay was also part of the project but opted out when he was fifteen. For Suman, being photographed daily feels normal, though sometimes she finds it irritating, especially if she’s running late. Still, she feels all the photos are special and says, "I don't have a favorite because they all mean something to me." Suman is currently completing her A-levels and hopes to study to become a paediatric nurse at university. She wants to continue photography as a hobby but doubts she’ll keep up daily photos once she leaves home. Munish also expects the project to end soon, though he may continue a little longer if Suman wants to. The photographs capture Suman from her earliest days, through school years, and into young adulthood — each moment a testament to her father's dedication. As Suman turns 18, the remarkable portrait made from 6,575 photos celebrates not only her growth but the bond of family and memory.

article_content: In Jerusalem, Israelis woke to striking newspaper images of ultra-orthodox children wearing yellow stars and striped uniforms reminiscent of the Holocaust. These photos were taken at a Saturday night protest by a radical ultra-orthodox group objecting to what they called hostility from the media and government. This demonstration, which drew widespread condemnation, showcases growing discord between Haredim (ultra-orthodox Jews) and the wider Israeli population. Recent conflicts have focused on attempts by some Haredi members to impose strict gender segregation and modesty rules outside their own neighborhoods. In areas with large Haredi communities, men have demanded separate seating for men and women on public buses and in stores. Some billboards featuring women have been defaced, prompting advertisers to avoid using women's images. Public outrage intensified with the case of eight-year-old Naama Margolese in Beit Shemesh, who tearfully described her fear of walking to school because ultra-orthodox neighbors harassed her about her clothes. The story ignited criticism and led Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to condemn gender segregation as inconsistent with Jewish and democratic values. Thousands gathered in Beit Shemesh the following week, calling for stronger government action against ultra-orthodox extremism. Leaders from the ultra-orthodox community emphasize that their entire population should not be judged by the actions of a radical few and state their respect for the secular community’s lifestyle. Rabbi Shmuel Poppenheim of the Eda Haredit reiterated his stance against imposing ultra-orthodox customs on others. Yet, the gaps go deeper. The Haredim, who represent about 10% of Israelis, are also a potent political force. They have secured government support for Torah study and exemptions from compulsory military service, fueling frustration among secular Israelis. Writer Bradley Burston suggests the current situation is unsustainable and may deepen unless the ultra-orthodox community becomes more integrated into Israeli life.

article_content: In a unique tribute to the area’s past, a small Georgian-style house constructed entirely from paraffin wax bricks appeared on a patch of wasteland along London’s Southwark Street, just steps from Borough Market. Conceived by British artist and designer Alex Chinneck—renowned for his eye-catching optical illusions—the structure was built from around 8,000 wax bricks, each bonded with terracotta sand. The work took a year of collaboration with engineers and wax experts to perfect the look and solidity. Entitled 'A Pound Of Flesh For 50p (The Melting House),' the installation’s name subtly nods to a famous line from Shakespeare’s The Merchant of Venice. Meant to slowly disappear, the house has been methodically melted with industrial heat tools, enabling Chinneck to guide the melting process. This temporary installation pays homage to a candle factory that operated in the neighborhood more than a century ago. Part of this year’s Merge Festival—a London event highlighting the area’s heritage through art, music, and performance—the melting wax house stood for just over a month before being reduced to a puddle and scheduled for removal. The spectacle drew attention for its creative blending of history, transformation, and public art.

article_content: Thousands of family doctors will receive their salaries despite going on strike this Thursday. Health trusts have chosen not to withhold pay, even though GPs will refuse to treat most patients, citing that urgent cases will still be seen. A day's pay for a GP earning £110,000 annually is about £430. Members of the British Medical Association (BMA) are striking to protest changes to their pension scheme, which would grant a pension of £68,000 per year. A senior official at one NHS trust commented: 'This sends a message to doctors that they can take any action they want and still be paid. My colleagues and I are extremely upset; this seems completely unjust.' The strike is expected to lead to the cancellation of around 1.25 million appointments, tests, and operations. At least 40 percent of doctors are likely to participate, affecting both hospitals and local surgeries. Daniel Poulter, a Conservative MP and hospital doctor, said: 'A doctor's primary duty is to care for patients, but this strike will result in cancelled operations and could put patients' lives at risk. The public will be shocked to learn doctors will still be paid on the day of the strike. If doctors decide to strike, they should not accept their pay for that day.' Employers are generally allowed to withhold or reduce pay for those who strike or only perform limited duties, but at least nine of England's 50 primary care trusts have chosen not to cut GPs' pay, mainly due to administrative challenges. GPs are usually self-employed and paid by surgeries, while hospital doctors are employees who will generally lose pay unless they make up the hours. None of the 25 organizations contacted by the Mail said they would dock GPs' pay. Trusts not cutting pay include Buckingham and Oxfordshire, Bristol, Berkshire, Derbyshire, Nottingham, South-West Essex, Sussex, Cheshire, Warrington, and Wirral. Andrew Lansley, Secretary of State for Health, encouraged GPs to open surgeries on Saturday to help manage the backlog. NHS Stockport suggested it was unlikely any pay would be deducted, as trusts find calculating such deductions too difficult. Dean Royles, head of NHS Employers, noted that doctors' work can be complex, with many still handling urgent cases during the strike. Some organizations are making arrangements for proportional deductions, recognizing pay for partial performance. He explained, 'This usually involves a deduction for the part of the day not worked.' Staff not joining the action will be paid as normal. Royles also stated that doctors who reschedule clinics for other days, such as Friday mornings, would still receive their pay, though they would have to catch up on paperwork at another time. Some hospitals plan to deduct between 30 and 50 percent of pay for staff striking on Thursday, while other sites will not pay striking doctors for that day at all. Last week, Lansley wrote to BMA council chair Hamish Meldrum, highlighting that today's routine appointments could become tomorrow’s emergencies. Meldrum responded that patient safety would not be put at risk, saying the action is motivated by a strong feeling among doctors that the pension changes are unfair and unnecessary. He emphasized that doctors will be present in their workplaces and that patient safety remains their highest priority. The BMA has not confirmed if GPs will work on Saturday but insists any missed work will be made up later. However, most GPs are unlikely to work weekends since a 2004 contract let them opt out of weekend hours. Doctors note that they contribute a higher proportion of their salary to pensions than other NHS staff. A BMA spokesperson noted that the decision to pay striking doctors is up to each individual trust.

article_content: CNN Student News – September 7, 2010 Today's program includes stories from New Zealand, Guatemala, and Chile. Anchor Carl Azuz welcomes viewers back after Labor Day and introduces the main topics.  First Up: Focus on the Economy President Barack Obama discussed the ongoing economic recovery, pointing out that eight million Americans lost jobs during the recession. Despite eight consecutive months of private sector job growth, the pace hasn't been fast enough. Obama highlighted transportation infrastructure projects as part of efforts to boost employment and the economy. The current U.S. unemployment rate is 9.6%, up slightly from last month. All proposed transportation projects require congressional approval, and some analysts believe rapid progress is unlikely. A CNN poll shows nearly 60% of Americans disapprove of the president's handling of the economy.  Midterm Elections Job creation and the economy are expected to be major issues in the upcoming midterm elections on November 2. Every seat in the U.S. House of Representatives and 37 out of 100 Senate seats are up for election, along with 37 governorships. In a recent CNN/Opinion Research Corporation Poll, 52% of likely voters favored Republicans while 45% supported Democrats. Another poll found that 81% of Americans view the U.S. economy as being in poor condition.  Blowout Preventer Raised Officials investigating the Gulf of Mexico oil spill have removed the failed blowout preventer for analysis. A replacement device has been installed, and after testing, authorities plan to drill the remaining distance of a relief well to permanently seal the original well.  I.D. Me New Zealand, an island nation southeast of Australia, has about 4 million residents and Wellington as its capital.  New Zealand Quake Parts of New Zealand are recovering after a 7.1 magnitude earthquake hit last weekend. A few people sustained serious injuries and around 100 others had minor injuries, but no deaths were reported. Over 5,000 property damage claims have been submitted, mainly for homes. Aftershocks are ongoing and could continue for up to a week.  Guatemala Landslides Guatemala is experiencing its heaviest rainfall in sixty years, leading to deadly landslides. Over 40,000 people are at risk, and dozens have been killed or injured. In one incident, a landslide knocked vehicles off the road, and a second slide hit rescuers at the same location. Thousands of homes and many fields have been destroyed. The president has declared a national emergency and a day of mourning.  Chile Miners Rescue efforts continue for 33 Chilean miners trapped underground. Officials are pursuing three plans: drilling straight down, drilling at an angle, and using an oil drill. These measures aim to bring the miners to safety, though some options may take several months.  What's the Word? – Loiter The word 'loiter' means to remain in an area without a specific purpose.  Anti-Loitering Device A mall in Washington, D.C. is using the 'Mosquito,' a device that emits a high-pitched noise mostly audible to people aged 13 to 25. While property managers insist it does not specifically target teens, the device is intended to reduce loitering, which can impact businesses. Some community leaders argue that better youth engagement programs would be a more positive solution.  Before We Go Competitive eater Sonya Thomas, known as 'The Black Widow,' set a new record by eating 181 chicken wings in 12 minutes at an event in Buffalo, New York.  Closing Carl Azuz concludes the show with puns and encourages viewers to return for more news.
